topics.name: Human Biology and Physiology
concepts: Liver: largest gland, makes bile and urea, stores vitamin A, detoxifies most drugs; Kupffer cells are its macrophages [repeat]
Peyer's patches = lymphoid tissue of ileum; Brunner's glands = duodenal submucosa [repeat]
Enterokinase activates trypsinogen; HCl activates pepsinogen; bile emulsifies fat, has no enzyme
O₂ travels as oxyhaemoglobin (~97%); CO₂ mostly as HCO₃⁻ (~70%) with chloride shift [repeat]
High altitude → erythropoietin → more RBCs; breathing driven mainly by rising CO₂/H⁺ at medulla [repeat]
Heart is myogenic: SA node in right atrium is pacemaker; SA → AV → His → Purkinje [repeat]
Eustachian valve guards inferior vena cava in right atrium; lub = AV valves close, dub = semilunar [repeat]
Pulse = heart rate; cardiac output = HR × SV ≈ 5 L/min; one cycle at 75/min = 0.8 s [repeat]
ABO: O universal donor, AB universal recipient; IᴬI° × IᴮIᴮ gives AB or B children [repeat]
Ultrafiltration driven by glomerular hydrostatic pressure (efferent narrower than afferent); GFR ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day [repeat]
PCT reabsorbs all glucose; ascending Henle impermeable to water; ADH and aldosterone act on DCT/collecting duct
Resting potential −70 mV (K⁺ leak, Na⁺–K⁺ pump 3 out/2 in); Na⁺ influx depolarises; synapse uses acetylcholine [repeat]
Cerebrum: memory, reasoning; cerebellum: balance; hypothalamus: temperature, thirst; medulla: heart and breathing centres [repeat]
Eye coats: sclera, choroid (pigmented), retina; cones = colour; crista = rotation, macula = static balance [repeat]
Cushing's = excess cortisol; Addison's = low adrenal cortex; cretinism vs myxoedema; acromegaly vs gigantism [repeat]
Sertoli cells nourish sperms; Leydig make testosterone; sperm mitochondria in middle piece; ovulation by LH surge [repeat]

topics.name: Microbial Diseases and Immunology
concepts: Typhoid: Salmonella typhi, faeco-oral, Widal test [repeat]
TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Koch); Mantoux test; BCG = live attenuated
HIV: RNA retrovirus, reverse transcriptase, kills CD4 helper T cells; ELISA; not spread by mosquitoes or touch [repeat]
Cholera: Vibrio cholerae, rice-water stools; ORS works by Na⁺–glucose cotransport
Influenza: RNA virus, droplets; yearly vaccine due to H and N antigen changes
Hepatitis A, E faeco-oral; B, C, D via blood; HBV vaccine is recombinant HBsAg from yeast
Candidiasis: Candida albicans; after antibiotics, HIV, diabetes
Innate immunity: skin, mucus, lysozyme, phagocytes; acquired: B (humoral) and T (cell-mediated)
Antibody = 2 heavy + 2 light chains; IgG crosses placenta, IgA in colostrum, IgE allergy, IgM first/largest
Vaccine → artificial active; antiserum/antivenom → artificial passive; colostrum → natural passive
Live attenuated: BCG, MMR, Sabin OPV; inactivated: Salk IPV; toxoid: tetanus, diphtheria
Benign tumour stays localised; malignant tumour metastasises; oncology = study of tumours [repeat]

topics.name: Medical Technology and Applied Biology
concepts: Autograft (self), isograft (identical twin), allograft (same species), xenograft (other species)
Rejection is T-cell response to HLA (MHC); cyclosporin A suppresses it
IVF: fertilisation in lab dish, embryo transferred; ICSI injects one sperm into ovum
Amniocentesis: amniotic fluid at 15–20 weeks; detects chromosomal disorders like Down syndrome
Transgenic animal carries foreign gene; Rosie cow (1997) gave milk with human α-lactalbumin
Lactobacillus: curd; Saccharomyces cerevisiae: beer, wine, bread; Propionibacterium shermanii: Swiss cheese holes
Secondary sewage treatment: aerobic flocs lower BOD; anaerobic sludge digesters make biogas (methane)
High BOD = high organic pollution; chlorination kills microbes in drinking water
Bio-control: Bt (Cry toxin) for insect larvae, Trichoderma for plant fungi, Gambusia for mosquito larvae
Cyclosporin A comes from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum

questions.q: The dental formula of an adult human is
questions.x: Each half-jaw has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars: 8 × 4 = 32 teeth.
questions.trap: 2102/2102 is the milk-teeth formula of a child.
questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands

questions.q: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by
questions.x: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the intestinal mucosa converts inactive trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates more trypsinogen.
questions.trap: HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach, not trypsinogen.

questions.q: Castle's intrinsic factor, needed for absorption of vitamin B₁₂, is secreted by
questions.x: Parietal cells of gastric glands secrete HCl and intrinsic factor; lack of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anaemia.
questions.trap: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and rennin, not intrinsic factor.
questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands

questions.q: Kwashiorkor in children results mainly from deficiency of
questions.x: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency with roughly adequate calories: oedema, swollen belly, skin and hair changes. Deficiency of both protein and calories causes marasmus.

questions.q: Most carbon dioxide (about 70%) is transported in blood as
questions.x: Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs forms H₂CO₃, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. About 70% goes as bicarbonate, 20–25% as carbamino compounds, 7% dissolved.
questions.trap: Carboxyhaemoglobin is carbon monoxide bound to Hb, not CO₂.
questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport

questions.q: A person has tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 3000 mL, expiratory reserve volume 1100 mL and residual volume 1200 mL. The vital capacity is
questions.x: VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3000 + 1100 = 4600 mL. Adding residual volume gives total lung capacity, 5800 mL.
questions.trap: 5800 mL is total lung capacity; vital capacity excludes residual volume.

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes
o: increased O₂ affinity of haemoglobin at high pCO₂
release of CO₂ from haemoglobin when it binds O₂
movement of chloride ions into RBCs
decreased O₂ affinity of haemoglobin when pCO₂ rises and pH falls
questions.x: High pCO₂ and H⁺ in tissues shift the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin unloads more oxygen where it is needed.
questions.trap: Chloride shift and the Haldane effect are separate CO₂-transport events.
questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport

questions.q: A person with blood group AB has
o: anti-A and anti-B antibodies but no antigens
both A and B antigens and no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
only antigen A and anti-B antibodies
questions.x: AB red cells carry both A and B antigens, so the plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B; hence AB is the universal recipient in the ABO system.
questions.trap: Group O, not AB, has both antibodies and no antigens.
questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure

questions.q: Erythroblastosis foetalis is most likely when
o: mother is Rh⁺ and foetus is Rh⁻
mother is Rh⁻ and foetus is Rh⁺, in a second pregnancy
both mother and foetus are Rh⁻
mother is Rh⁻ and foetus is Rh⁻, in a first pregnancy
questions.x: An Rh⁻ mother sensitised by Rh⁺ foetal blood (usually at the first delivery) makes anti-Rh antibodies that cross the placenta in the next Rh⁺ pregnancy and destroy foetal RBCs.
questions.trap: The first Rh⁺ pregnancy is usually safe; sensitisation happens at delivery.
questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure

questions.q: In a normal ECG, the QRS complex represents
questions.x: P wave = atrial depolarisation; QRS complex = ventricular depolarisation (start of ventricular systole); T wave = ventricular repolarisation.
questions.trap: The T wave, not QRS, shows ventricular repolarisation.
questions.s: Circulatory system: heart, cardiac cycle and output

questions.q: If heart rate is 72 beats/min and stroke volume is 70 mL, the cardiac output is about
questions.x: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 72 × 70 = 5040 mL/min ≈ 5.0 L/min.
questions.s: Circulatory system: heart, cardiac cycle and output

questions.q: The counter-current mechanism that helps produce concentrated urine operates mainly between
o: Loop of Henle and vasa recta
questions.x: Opposite flow in the limbs of Henle's loop and in the vasa recta builds and keeps a rising osmotic gradient in the medulla, so water leaves the collecting duct under ADH.

questions.q: In a healthy adult, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about
questions.x: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min, i.e., 125 × 1440 ≈ 180 litres of filtrate per day, of which about 99% is reabsorbed.
questions.trap: 180 is litres per day, not mL per minute.

questions.q: A fall in glomerular blood pressure stimulates the juxtaglomerular cells to release
questions.x: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then ACE forms angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, restoring pressure and GFR.
questions.trap: Aldosterone comes later, from the adrenal cortex, not from JG cells.

questions.q: In each cycle, the Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase pump of a neuron moves
questions.x: Using one ATP, the pump expels 3 Na⁺ and brings in 2 K⁺, helping keep the resting potential (about −70 mV, inside negative).

questions.q: Damage to which part of the brain causes loss of balance and muscular coordination?
questions.x: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements and maintains posture and equilibrium.
questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic

questions.q: Rhodopsin (visual purple) of rod cells is made of opsin and
questions.x: Rhodopsin = opsin + retinal (vitamin A aldehyde). Vitamin A deficiency lowers rhodopsin and causes night blindness.

questions.q: The organ of Corti, the receptor for hearing, lies in the
questions.x: The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane inside the cochlea; semicircular canals and utriculus deal with balance.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by
questions.x: β-cells secrete insulin (lowers blood glucose); α-cells secrete glucagon (raises it); δ-cells secrete somatostatin; acinar cells make digestive enzymes.

questions.q: Diabetes insipidus is caused by deficiency of
questions.x: Without ADH, the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb little water, so large volumes of dilute urine are passed, without glucose.
questions.trap: Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus, with sugar in urine.

questions.q: Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) results from
questions.x: Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism: high metabolic rate, weight loss, nervousness and protruding eyeballs.
questions.trap: Child hypothyroidism is cretinism; iodine deficiency causes simple goitre.

questions.q: The hormone that raises the blood calcium level is
questions.x: Parathormone increases bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption. Calcitonin from thyroid C-cells lowers blood Ca²⁺.
questions.trap: Calcitonin does the opposite: it lowers blood calcium.

questions.q: During contraction of a skeletal muscle fibre, which part of the sarcomere does NOT change in length?
questions.x: Actin slides over myosin. The A-band equals the length of the myosin filaments, so it stays constant while the I-band, H-zone and sarcomere shorten.
questions.trap: H-zone is chosen often, but it shortens or disappears.

questions.q: In muscle contraction, Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to
questions.x: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin so cross-bridges can form.
questions.trap: Tropomyosin moves, but Ca²⁺ binds troponin.

questions.q: Floating ribs in humans are the
questions.x: Ribs 1–7 (true) join the sternum directly; 8–10 (false) join through the 7th costal cartilage; 11–12 are floating, free ventrally.
questions.trap: 8th to 10th are false (vertebrochondral) ribs, not floating.

questions.q: How many sperms and ova are produced from 10 primary spermatocytes and 10 primary oocytes respectively?
questions.x: Each primary spermatocyte gives 4 sperms (10 × 4 = 40); each primary oocyte gives only 1 ovum plus polar bodies (10 × 1 = 10).
questions.trap: 40 and 40 forgets that polar bodies are not ova.

questions.q: Testosterone is secreted by
questions.x: Leydig cells lying between seminiferous tubules secrete testosterone under the influence of LH.
questions.trap: Sertoli cells nourish sperms and secrete inhibin, not testosterone.

questions.q: Ovulation in the human menstrual cycle is triggered by a mid-cycle surge of
questions.x: A sharp LH surge around day 14 of a 28-day cycle ruptures the Graafian follicle; the remnant becomes the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum.
questions.trap: FSH also rises slightly, but LH is the ovulation trigger.
questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle

questions.q: The acrosome of a human sperm
o: contains lytic enzymes that help penetrate the egg's coverings
forms the axial filament of the tail
questions.x: The acrosome, formed from the Golgi apparatus, holds hydrolytic enzymes (sperm lysins such as hyaluronidase) that dissolve the egg's coverings.
questions.trap: Energy comes from mitochondria of the middle piece.

questions.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the
questions.x: Sperm meet the secondary oocyte in the ampulla (ampullary–isthmic region) of the fallopian tube; the zygote then moves to the uterus for implantation.
questions.trap: The uterus is the site of implantation, not fertilisation.

questions.q: Which of the following is derived from mesoderm?
questions.x: Mesoderm forms muscles, heart, blood, kidneys, gonads and dermis. Brain and epidermis are ectodermal; gut lining is endodermal.

questions.q: In the human blastocyst, the inner cell mass gives rise to
questions.x: The inner cell mass (embryoblast) differentiates into the embryo; the outer trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and helps form the placenta.

questions.q: HIV mainly destroys
questions.x: HIV, a retrovirus, enters helper T cells through CD4, copies itself with reverse transcriptase and kills them, collapsing immunity (AIDS).

questions.q: The Widal test is used to diagnose
questions.x: The Widal test detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi antigens in the patient's serum. ELISA is used for HIV.

questions.q: Antibodies received by a newborn through colostrum provide
questions.x: The baby receives ready-made antibodies (mainly IgA) instead of making them, so it is passive; it happens naturally through feeding, so natural passive.
questions.trap: Active immunity needs the baby's own antibody production.

questions.q: The only antibody class that crosses the human placenta is
questions.x: IgG, the most abundant and a small monomeric antibody, crosses the placenta and protects the foetus.
questions.trap: IgA reaches the baby in colostrum, not across the placenta.

questions.q: Dengue fever is transmitted by
questions.x: Dengue virus is spread by the day-biting Aedes aegypti mosquito; it causes high fever, severe joint pain and a fall in platelet count.
questions.trap: Anopheles transmits malaria, not dengue.

questions.q: The spread of cancer cells from the original tumour to distant parts of the body is called
questions.x: Malignant cells lose contact inhibition, invade tissues and travel in blood or lymph to form secondary tumours — metastasis.
questions.trap: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not spread.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: The largest gland of the human body is the
questions.x: The liver (about 1.5 kg in adults) is the largest gland; it secretes bile and stores glycogen, iron and fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Kupffer cells, which engulf old blood cells and bacteria, are found in the
questions.x: Kupffer cells are fixed macrophages lining the sinusoids of the liver.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Most drugs and toxic substances are detoxified (metabolised) in the human body by the
questions.x: Hepatocytes contain drug-metabolising enzymes that convert drugs and toxins into less harmful, water-soluble products, which the kidney then excretes.
questions.trap: Kidney excretes the products but does not mainly metabolise drugs.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Vitamin A is stored mainly in the
questions.x: The liver stores fat-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin A (and D, B₁₂, iron); this is why liver oils are rich in vitamin A.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Peyer's patches are
o: Lymphoid follicles in the wall of the ileum
Mucous glands in the submucosa of the duodenum
questions.x: Peyer's patches are aggregates of lymphoid tissue in the ileum; they produce lymphocytes and guard against gut microbes.
questions.trap: Mucous glands of duodenal submucosa are Brunner's glands.

questions.q: Bile helps in the digestion of fats by
questions.x: Bile has no digestive enzyme. Its bile salts emulsify fat, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase.
questions.trap: Lipase, not bile, hydrolyses fats.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Brunner's glands are located in the
questions.x: Brunner's glands lie in the duodenal submucosa and secrete alkaline mucus that protects the duodenum from acidic chyme.

questions.q: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) converts starch mainly into
questions.x: Ptyalin acts at about pH 6.8 and breaks starch into maltose (and dextrins); maltase later converts maltose to glucose.
questions.trap: Glucose forms only later, by maltase in the intestine.

questions.q: Rennin, present in the gastric juice of infants, acts on
questions.x: Rennin coagulates soluble milk protein caseinogen into casein (curdling), so milk stays longer in the stomach for pepsin to act.

questions.q: Digested fats are absorbed into lymph vessels of the villi called
questions.x: Fatty acids and glycerol are re-formed into fat, packed as chylomicrons and enter the lacteals (lymph), not blood directly.

questions.q: The hormone that causes the gall bladder to contract and release bile is
questions.x: Fat and protein in the duodenum release CCK, which contracts the gall bladder and stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic juice.
questions.trap: Secretin mainly stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Yellowing of the skin and eyes in jaundice is due to deposition of
questions.x: Bilirubin, a yellow bile pigment from haemoglobin breakdown, accumulates in blood and tissues when the liver or bile flow fails.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: About 97% of the oxygen in blood is transported
o: As oxyhaemoglobin in red blood cells
questions.x: Each haemoglobin carries up to 4 O₂ molecules as oxyhaemoglobin; only about 3% of O₂ is dissolved in plasma.

questions.q: The basic rhythm of breathing is set by the respiratory centre located in the
questions.x: The rhythm centre is in the medulla oblongata; the pneumotaxic centre in the pons fine-tunes the rate.

questions.q: In a healthy person, the rate of breathing increases mainly in response to a rise in blood
questions.x: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to rising CO₂ and H⁺; low O₂ becomes the main drive only when it falls very low.
questions.trap: A fall, not a rise, in O₂ stimulates breathing.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: A person who stays for some weeks at a high altitude shows
o: A decrease in red blood cell count
An increase in red blood cell count
questions.x: Low pO₂ at altitude makes the kidney release erythropoietin, which increases RBC production in bone marrow (polycythaemia), improving O₂ carriage.

questions.q: The number of lobes in the right and left human lungs is
questions.x: The right lung has 3 lobes; the left has 2 lobes, leaving space for the heart (cardiac notch).
questions.trap: 2 and 3 reverses the sides.

questions.q: Surfactant secreted by alveolar cells
o: Lowers surface tension and prevents alveoli from collapsing
Carries oxygen across the alveolar wall
Raises surface tension in the alveoli
questions.x: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant (a phospholipid); its lack in premature babies causes respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: During CO₂ transport, chloride ions move into red blood cells in exchange for
questions.x: HCO₃⁻ formed inside RBCs diffuses into plasma; Cl⁻ moves in to keep electrical balance. This is the chloride (Hamburger) shift.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: The enzyme in red blood cells that speeds up the reaction CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ is
questions.x: Carbonic anhydrase, a zinc enzyme, makes bicarbonate transport of CO₂ fast in tissues and its release fast in lungs.

questions.s: Respiratory system: concept of respiratory disorders
questions.q: Breakdown of alveolar walls that reduces the surface area for gas exchange, mainly due to smoking, is called
questions.x: In emphysema alveoli merge into large sacs, so the respiratory surface falls; cigarette smoking is the major cause.
questions.trap: Asthma narrows bronchioles; it does not destroy alveolar walls.

questions.s: Respiratory system: concept of respiratory disorders
questions.q: Asthma is characterised by
o: Spasm and narrowing of the bronchioles, causing wheezing
Scarring of lungs from silica dust
Filling of alveoli with pus due to bacteria
questions.x: Asthma is an allergic inflammation in which bronchiole muscles contract and mucus increases, making breathing (especially expiration) difficult.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: Carbon monoxide is poisonous mainly because it
o: Binds haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen does
questions.x: CO binds haemoglobin about 200 times more firmly than O₂, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin, so less O₂ reaches tissues.

questions.q: A resting person has a tidal volume of 500 mL and breathes 12 times per minute. The pulmonary (minute) ventilation is
questions.x: Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate = 500 × 12 = 6000 mL/min (6 L/min).

questions.q: During normal inspiration
o: The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped
Pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure
questions.x: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarges the thoracic cavity; lung pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in.
questions.trap: A relaxed, dome-shaped diaphragm belongs to expiration.

questions.q: The human heart is called myogenic because
o: Its beat is started by a specialised muscle tissue, the SA node
Its beat is started by the vagus nerve
Its beat is started by the cardiac centre of the brain
Its beat is started by adrenaline
questions.x: Impulses arise in the heart itself, in the SA node (pacemaker). Nerves and hormones only change the rate.
questions.trap: The vagus slows the heart; it does not start the beat.

questions.q: The sino-atrial (SA) node lies in the
o: Wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava
Wall of the left atrium near the pulmonary veins
questions.x: The SA node sits in the upper right atrial wall near the superior vena cava; the AV node lies near the interatrial septum.

questions.q: The Eustachian valve of the human heart is found
o: At the opening of the coronary sinus
Between the left atrium and left ventricle
In the right atrium at the opening of the inferior vena cava
At the base of the aorta
questions.x: The Eustachian valve guards the opening of the inferior vena cava into the right atrium; the Thebesian valve guards the coronary sinus.
questions.trap: Don't confuse it with the Eustachian tube of the ear.

questions.q: The bicuspid (mitral) valve is present between the
questions.x: The bicuspid valve has two cusps and guards the left atrioventricular opening; the tricuspid guards the right one.

questions.q: The first heart sound 'lub' is produced by
o: Closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves
questions.x: 'Lub' marks the start of ventricular systole as AV valves close; 'dub' is closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole.
questions.trap: Semilunar valve closure gives the second sound, 'dub'.

questions.q: Counting the pulse at the wrist directly gives a person's
questions.x: Each ventricular contraction sends a pressure wave along the arteries; the number of pulses per minute equals the heart rate (about 72/min).

questions.q: If the heart beats 75 times per minute, the duration of one cardiac cycle is
questions.x: Duration = 60 s ÷ 75 = 0.8 s.

questions.q: In a blood pressure reading of 120/80 mm Hg, 80 represents the
questions.x: The upper value (120) is systolic pressure during ventricular contraction; the lower (80) is diastolic pressure during relaxation.

questions.q: A person's blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. The pulse pressure is
questions.x: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 130 − 85 = 45 mm Hg.
questions.trap: 100 mm Hg is the mean arterial pressure (85 + 45/3).

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: The vessels that carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart are the
questions.x: Four pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
questions.trap: Pulmonary arteries are arteries carrying deoxygenated blood.

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the
questions.x: It brings absorbed food-rich blood from the stomach and intestines to the liver for processing before it reaches the heart.
questions.trap: Liver to heart is the hepatic vein.

questions.q: The most abundant white blood cells, which are actively phagocytic, are
questions.x: Neutrophils form about 60–70% of WBCs and are the first phagocytes to reach infected sites.

questions.q: During blood clotting, thrombin converts
questions.x: Thromboplastin with Ca²⁺ turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin then converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap cells.
questions.trap: Prothrombin to thrombin is the step before, done by thromboplastin.

questions.q: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting because it is required for
o: Absorption of calcium from the gut
Production of platelets in bone marrow
Synthesis of prothrombin in the liver
questions.x: The liver needs vitamin K to make prothrombin and other clotting factors; its deficiency delays clotting.

questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure
questions.q: A mother of genotype IᴮIᴮ and a father of blood group A (genotype not known) can have children of blood group
questions.x: Father is IᴬIᴬ or IᴬI°. IᴬIᴬ × IᴮIᴮ gives only AB; IᴬI° × IᴮIᴮ gives AB (IᴬIᴮ) or B (IᴮI°). Group A or O is impossible.
questions.trap: AB only assumes the father is surely IᴬIᴬ.

questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure
questions.q: In the ABO system, the universal donor blood group is
questions.x: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so they are not agglutinated by recipients' anti-A or anti-B.
questions.trap: AB is the universal recipient, not donor.

questions.q: Deposition of cholesterol plaques in the inner walls of arteries, narrowing them, is called
questions.x: Atherosclerosis narrows arteries and raises blood pressure; in coronary arteries it can cause angina and heart attack.
questions.trap: Angina is the chest pain that results, not the deposit itself.

questions.q: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) results from
o: Failure of the SA node only
Blockage of a coronary artery so that part of the heart muscle dies
questions.x: When a coronary artery is blocked (often by a clot on a plaque), the heart muscle it supplies is deprived of O₂ and dies.

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: Compared with blood, lymph has
o: No red blood cells and less protein
questions.x: Lymph is tissue fluid collected by lymph vessels: it has lymphocytes but no RBCs and fewer proteins than plasma.

questions.q: A person's cardiac output is 6 L/min and stroke volume is 80 mL. The heart rate is
questions.x: Heart rate = cardiac output ÷ stroke volume = 6000 mL ÷ 80 mL = 75 beats/min.

questions.q: The correct order of conduction of the cardiac impulse is
o: AV node → SA node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
SA node → bundle of His → AV node → Purkinje fibres
Purkinje fibres → bundle of His → AV node → SA node
questions.x: The impulse starts at the SA node, spreads over the atria to the AV node, then down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres into ventricular walls.

questions.q: Red blood cells live about 120 days, and old ones are mostly destroyed in the
questions.x: The spleen, the 'graveyard of RBCs', removes worn-out red cells; their haemoglobin is broken down to bilirubin.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule is caused mainly by
o: Action of ADH on the glomerulus
High hydrostatic (blood) pressure in the glomerulus
questions.x: Glomerular blood pressure forces water and small solutes through the filtration membrane; plasma protein osmotic pressure opposes filtration.
questions.trap: Plasma protein osmotic pressure opposes, not drives, filtration.

questions.q: Blood pressure in the glomerulus stays high mainly because
o: The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole
The afferent arteriole is narrower than the efferent arteriole
Blood enters the glomerulus from a vein
questions.x: Blood enters by a wider afferent arteriole and leaves by a narrower efferent arteriole, so pressure builds up (about 60 mm Hg) for filtration.

questions.q: Glucose in the glomerular filtrate is normally reabsorbed completely in the
questions.x: The PCT reabsorbs about 65–70% of filtrate, including all glucose and amino acids, by active transport.

questions.q: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle
o: Is permeable to water but not to salts
Is permeable to both water and salts
Is impermeable to water but moves NaCl out into the medulla
questions.x: The descending limb lets water out; the ascending limb pumps out NaCl but keeps water in, so filtrate becomes dilute while the medulla becomes salty.
questions.trap: Water-permeable but salt-impermeable describes the descending limb.

questions.q: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to
o: Increase reabsorption of Na⁺ (and secretion of K⁺)
questions.x: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex retains Na⁺ and water and removes K⁺, raising blood volume and pressure.

questions.q: In humans, urea is synthesised in the
questions.x: Liver cells convert ammonia and CO₂ to urea in the ornithine (urea) cycle; kidneys only remove it. Humans are ureotelic.
questions.trap: Kidneys excrete urea; they do not make it.

questions.s: Excretory system: concept of renal disorders
questions.q: Most kidney stones (renal calculi) are made of
questions.x: Most renal stones are crystals of calcium oxalate; they can block urine flow and cause severe pain.

questions.s: Excretory system: concept of renal disorders
questions.q: In kidney failure, haemodialysis removes from the blood mainly
o: Urea and other small waste molecules
questions.x: Blood flows past a semipermeable membrane in dialysing fluid; small solutes like urea diffuse out while cells and proteins stay in.

questions.s: Excretory system: concept of renal disorders
questions.q: Presence of glucose in urine (glycosuria) is most commonly a sign of
questions.x: When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (about 180 mg/dL) in diabetes mellitus, tubules cannot reabsorb all glucose.
questions.trap: Diabetes insipidus gives large volumes of urine without glucose.

questions.q: Each human kidney contains about
questions.x: Each kidney has roughly one million nephrons, its structural and functional units.

questions.q: About 180 L of glomerular filtrate forms per day and 1.8 L of urine is passed. The percentage of filtrate reabsorbed is
questions.x: Urine = 1.8/180 = 1% of filtrate, so 100 − 1 = 99% is reabsorbed.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is mainly due to the membrane being, at rest, more permeable to
questions.x: At rest many K⁺ leak channels are open, so K⁺ diffuses out and leaves the inside negative (about −70 mV); Na⁺ channels stay mostly closed.
questions.trap: Na⁺ permeability rises only during depolarisation.

questions.q: Depolarisation of a neuron during an action potential is caused by
o: Exit of K⁺ from the axon
Rapid entry of Na⁺ into the axon
Entry of Cl⁻ into the axon
Exit of Ca²⁺ from the axon
questions.x: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ rushes in and the inside becomes positive (about +30 mV). K⁺ exit then repolarises it.
questions.trap: K⁺ exit causes repolarisation, not depolarisation.

questions.q: At a chemical synapse, the nerve impulse passes to the next neuron by
o: Direct flow of electric current through a fused membrane
A neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine released into the synaptic cleft
Movement of the axon into the next neuron
questions.x: The arriving impulse opens Ca²⁺ channels; vesicles release a neurotransmitter that diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors on the next neuron.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Intelligence, memory, reasoning and voluntary actions are controlled by the
questions.x: The cerebral cortex is the seat of thinking, memory, attention, learning and voluntary movement.
questions.trap: Cerebellum coordinates movement but does not do reasoning.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The thermoregulatory (body temperature) centre of the brain is the
questions.x: The hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary gland.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The corpus callosum is a band of nerve fibres that connects the
questions.x: The corpus callosum, the largest commissure, links the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Humans have
o: 10 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
10 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
questions.x: Humans (mammals) have 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
questions.trap: 10 cranial pairs is the frog, not humans.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The vagus nerve, which slows the heart and supplies the lungs and gut, is the
questions.x: The vagus (X) is the longest cranial nerve and carries most parasympathetic fibres to thoracic and abdominal organs.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system causes
o: Increased heart rate and dilation of the pupils
questions.x: The sympathetic system prepares for 'fight or flight': faster heart, dilated pupils and bronchioles, slower digestion.
questions.trap: Pupil constriction and peristalsis are parasympathetic effects.

questions.q: Conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre is fast because the impulse
o: Travels through the myelin sheath itself
Jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
Is carried by blood around the nerve
questions.x: Myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier; this saltatory conduction is much faster.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The meninges covering the brain, from outside to inside, are
questions.x: Tough dura mater lies outermost, then the web-like arachnoid, then the thin vascular pia mater on the brain surface.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Which statement about the medulla oblongata is correct?
o: It controls body temperature and thirst
It is the centre of memory and reasoning
It contains centres controlling heartbeat, breathing and vomiting
questions.x: The medulla holds the cardiac, respiratory and vasomotor centres, plus reflex centres for vomiting, coughing and swallowing; damage is often fatal.
questions.trap: Temperature and thirst belong to the hypothalamus.

questions.q: The middle, vascular and pigmented coat of the eyeball is the
questions.x: The eye wall has three coats: outer sclera (cornea in front), middle choroid (blood vessels, pigment), inner retina.

questions.q: The receptor for rotational (dynamic) balance is the
o: Crista in the ampulla of the semicircular canals
questions.x: Cristae in the ampullae sense head rotation; maculae of the utriculus and sacculus sense static position and linear movement.
questions.trap: Macula detects static balance, not rotation.

questions.q: The part of the retina that has no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves the eye, is the
questions.x: The blind spot (optic disc) lacks photoreceptors, so no image forms there; the fovea has only cones and gives sharpest vision.
questions.trap: Fovea has the most cones, not none.

questions.q: Colour vision in humans depends on
questions.x: Cones contain iodopsin and work in bright light for colour and detail; rods contain rhodopsin for dim light.

questions.q: The smallest bone in the human body is the
questions.x: The stapes (stirrup), an ear ossicle about 3 mm long, fits into the oval window of the inner ear.

questions.q: The Eustachian tube connects the
o: External ear to the middle ear
Middle ear to the inner ear
questions.x: It equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum, which is why ears 'pop' during take-off.

questions.q: Myopia (short-sightedness) is due to
o: An elongated eyeball, and is corrected by a convex lens
A shortened eyeball, and is corrected by a concave lens
An elongated eyeball, and is corrected by a concave lens
Loss of lens elasticity with age, and is corrected by a cylindrical lens
questions.x: In myopia the eyeball is too long, so distant images form in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens corrects it.
questions.trap: A shortened eyeball causes hypermetropia, corrected by convex lens.

questions.q: Accommodation of the eye for near and far vision is brought about by
o: The iris changing the size of the pupil
The retina moving forward and backward
Ciliary muscles changing the curvature of the lens
questions.x: Ciliary muscles contract to make the lens more convex for near objects and relax to flatten it for distant objects.
questions.trap: The iris controls light entry, not focusing.

questions.q: Moon face, fat on the trunk and high blood sugar due to excess cortisol is called
questions.x: Cushing's syndrome is hypersecretion of glucocorticoids (cortisol) by the adrenal cortex.
questions.trap: Addison's disease is the opposite: too little cortical hormone.

questions.q: Addison's disease is caused by
o: Hyposecretion of hormones of the adrenal cortex
questions.x: Low cortisol and aldosterone cause weakness, low blood pressure, salt loss and bronze pigmentation of skin.

questions.q: Excess growth hormone after the growth plates have closed (in adults) causes
questions.x: In adults, extra GH enlarges bones of the face, hands and feet (acromegaly); in children it causes gigantism.
questions.trap: Gigantism happens only when excess GH starts before growth stops.

questions.q: Hyposecretion of thyroxine in children causes
questions.x: Cretinism: stunted growth and mental retardation in children. Thyroxine deficiency in adults causes myxoedema.

questions.q: Contraction of the uterus during childbirth and ejection of milk are caused by
questions.x: Oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary, contracts uterine muscle and milk-gland myoepithelium.
questions.trap: Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it.

questions.q: The 'fight or flight' hormone adrenaline is secreted by the
questions.x: The adrenal medulla, stimulated by sympathetic nerves, releases adrenaline in emergencies, raising heart rate and blood glucose.

questions.q: Melatonin, which regulates the sleep–wake (day–night) cycle, is secreted by the
questions.x: The pineal body secretes melatonin mainly in darkness; it influences biological rhythms.

questions.q: The thymus gland helps immunity by
o: Maturing T-lymphocytes under the influence of thymosin
questions.x: Thymosin from the thymus helps T-lymphocytes mature; the gland is large in children and shrinks after puberty.

questions.q: Hormones released from the posterior pituitary are actually synthesised in the
questions.x: Oxytocin and ADH are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells, carried down their axons and stored in the posterior pituitary until release.
questions.trap: The posterior pituitary only stores and releases them.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers the blood glucose level?
questions.x: Insulin increases glucose uptake by cells and its storage as glycogen; glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol all raise blood glucose.

questions.q: Developing sperms in the seminiferous tubules receive nourishment from
questions.x: Sertoli (sustentacular) cells nourish and support developing sperms and secrete inhibin; Leydig cells secrete testosterone.
questions.trap: Leydig cells make testosterone, not nourishment.

questions.q: In a sperm, the mitochondria that supply energy for movement of the tail are located in the
questions.x: The middle piece has a spiral of mitochondria that produce ATP to beat the tail (flagellum), which propels the sperm.

questions.q: The number of chromosomes in a human secondary oocyte is
questions.x: The first meiotic division halves the number: the secondary oocyte (and first polar body) is haploid with 23 chromosomes.
questions.trap: 46 is the primary oocyte, before meiosis I is complete.

questions.q: At ovulation, the human female gamete released from the ovary is
o: A secondary oocyte arrested at metaphase II
A mature ovum that has completed meiosis II
A primary oocyte arrested at prophase I
questions.x: Meiosis I finishes just before ovulation; the secondary oocyte stays in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only if a sperm enters.
questions.trap: Meiosis II completes only after sperm entry.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: After ovulation, the ruptured Graafian follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which mainly secretes
questions.x: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen), which keeps the endometrium ready for implantation.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: Menstruation begins when
o: Oestrogen level rises in the follicular phase
Progesterone level falls as the corpus luteum degenerates
FSH level rises at the start of the cycle
questions.x: Without fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates; falling progesterone causes the endometrium to break down and shed as menstrual flow.
questions.trap: The LH surge causes ovulation, not menstruation.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: A woman has a regular menstrual cycle of 32 days. Since the luteal phase lasts about 14 days, ovulation is expected around day
questions.x: Ovulation ≈ cycle length − luteal phase = 32 − 14 = day 18.
questions.trap: Day 14 is correct only for a 28-day cycle.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: Home pregnancy test kits detect in urine the hormone
questions.x: hCG is made by the trophoblast/placenta soon after implantation; it maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.

questions.q: Sperms are produced in the
questions.x: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules; sperms then mature and are stored in the epididymis.
questions.trap: The epididymis stores and matures sperms but does not make them.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, oestrogen is secreted mainly by the
questions.x: Under FSH, growing follicles secrete oestrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase).
questions.trap: The corpus luteum forms only after ovulation.

questions.q: Spermiogenesis is the
o: Formation of spermatogonia from germ cells
Release of sperms from Sertoli cells
questions.x: Spermiogenesis is the change of round haploid spermatids into tailed sperms; release from Sertoli cells is spermiation.
questions.trap: Release of sperms is spermiation, not spermiogenesis.

questions.q: How many secondary spermatocytes and spermatids are formed from 25 primary spermatocytes?
questions.x: Each primary spermatocyte forms 2 secondary spermatocytes (meiosis I), which form 4 spermatids (meiosis II): 25 × 2 = 50 and 25 × 4 = 100.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: Ovulation is triggered by a surge of LH, which is secreted by the
questions.x: LH and FSH are gonadotropins of the anterior pituitary; the hypothalamus releases GnRH which controls them.
questions.trap: The hypothalamus makes GnRH, not LH itself.

questions.q: Typhoid fever is caused by
questions.x: Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi; it is diagnosed by the Widal test and blood culture.

questions.q: Typhoid spreads mainly through
o: Bite of the female Anopheles mosquito
Food and water contaminated with faeces of patients or carriers
questions.x: Typhoid is faeco-orally transmitted; houseflies and healthy carriers help spread it. Safe water and sanitation prevent it.

questions.q: Tuberculosis is caused by
questions.x: Robert Koch discovered the TB bacillus in 1882; M. leprae causes leprosy.
questions.trap: M. leprae is the same genus but causes leprosy.

questions.q: The BCG vaccine, given at birth to protect against tuberculosis, is a
questions.x: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) contains live but weakened Mycobacterium bovis.

questions.q: The Mantoux (tuberculin) skin test is used in diagnosing
questions.x: Tuberculin (PPD) injected into the skin produces a raised hard area in people sensitised to TB bacilli. Sputum is examined for acid-fast bacilli.

questions.q: HIV is NOT transmitted by
o: An infected mother to her baby
questions.x: HIV spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood or needles, and mother to child; it does not spread by insects, touch or sharing food.

questions.q: HIV makes DNA from its RNA genome with the enzyme
questions.x: HIV is a retrovirus; reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host cell's DNA.

questions.q: The usual screening test for HIV infection is
questions.x: ELISA detects anti-HIV antibodies; positive results are confirmed by Western blot or PCR. Widal is for typhoid, VDRL for syphilis.

questions.q: Profuse watery 'rice-water' stools with severe dehydration are typical of
questions.x: Cholera toxin of Vibrio cholerae makes the intestine pour out water and salts, causing rice-water stools and rapid dehydration.

questions.q: Glucose is added to oral rehydration solution (ORS) used in cholera mainly because
o: It is co-transported with Na⁺ in the intestine, and water follows
It stops the secretion of mucus
questions.x: Sodium–glucose cotransport in intestinal cells still works in cholera, so glucose pulls Na⁺ and then water into the body.
questions.trap: ORS does not kill bacteria; it replaces lost water and salts.

questions.q: Influenza is caused by
o: A bacterium spread by contaminated water
An RNA virus spread by respiratory droplets
A fungus spread by skin contact
questions.x: Influenza virus (orthomyxovirus) has a segmented RNA genome and spreads by coughing, sneezing and contact.

questions.q: A new influenza vaccine is needed almost every year because
o: Influenza vaccines are toxoids that lose potency
Humans cannot form memory cells against viruses
The virus becomes resistant to antibiotics
The virus frequently changes its surface antigens (haemagglutinin and neuraminidase)
questions.x: Mutations in H and N genes (antigenic drift) produce new strains that old antibodies do not recognise well.
questions.trap: Antibiotics never act on viruses.

questions.q: Hepatitis A and hepatitis E spread mainly through
questions.x: Hepatitis A and E viruses pass out in faeces and infect via contaminated food and water; B, C and D spread by blood and body fluids.
questions.trap: Blood transfusion spreads hepatitis B and C, not A or E.

questions.q: Hepatitis B virus is transmitted mainly through
questions.x: HBV spreads through transfusion, shared needles, sex and from mother to baby; it damages the liver and can lead to cirrhosis and cancer.

questions.q: The vaccine against hepatitis B is produced as a
o: Toxoid of the hepatitis B toxin
Recombinant vaccine of the viral surface antigen made in yeast
questions.x: The HBsAg gene is expressed in yeast; the purified surface protein is used as a safe subunit vaccine.

questions.q: Candidiasis (oral thrush) is caused by
questions.x: Candida albicans normally lives harmlessly in the mouth, gut and vagina; it overgrows when immunity or normal flora is reduced.

questions.q: Candidiasis commonly appears after long courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics because
o: Antibiotics kill normal bacteria that keep Candida in check
questions.x: Normal bacterial flora compete with Candida; when they are killed, the fungus overgrows. It is also common in HIV and diabetes.

questions.q: Lysozyme present in tears and saliva is a part of
questions.x: Innate barriers include skin, mucus, stomach acid and lysozyme, which breaks bacterial cell walls; they act on any microbe, without memory.

questions.q: An antibody molecule (IgG) is made of
o: One heavy and one light chain
Two heavy and two light polypeptide chains
questions.x: Antibodies are Y-shaped, with two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds (H₂L₂).

questions.q: Antibodies are secreted by
questions.x: Activated B-lymphocytes divide to form plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells.

questions.q: The antibody class mainly responsible for allergic reactions is
questions.x: IgE binds mast cells and basophils; on contact with an allergen they release histamine, causing allergy.

questions.q: The largest antibody, which is the first to appear in a primary immune response, is
questions.x: IgM is a pentamer, the largest antibody, and is produced first; IgG follows and dominates later.
questions.trap: IgG dominates later and in secondary responses.

questions.q: A booster dose of a vaccine gives a faster and stronger response because of
o: Memory cells formed after the first dose
questions.x: Memory B and T cells from the primary response recognise the antigen quickly, so the secondary response is quicker, larger and longer lasting.

questions.q: The tetanus vaccine (TT) is an example of a
questions.x: A toxoid is a bacterial toxin made harmless (e.g. by formalin) that still induces antitoxin antibodies; tetanus and diphtheria vaccines are toxoids.

questions.q: Which of these vaccines contains live attenuated viruses?
questions.x: MMR uses weakened live viruses. Salk's IPV is inactivated, tetanus is a toxoid and hepatitis B is a recombinant subunit vaccine.
questions.trap: Salk polio vaccine is inactivated; Sabin's oral vaccine is live.

questions.q: An injection of anti-snake venom provides
questions.x: Ready-made antibodies (from horses) are injected, so the body does not make them (passive), and it is given medically (artificial).
questions.trap: Vaccines give active immunity; antiserum gives passive.

questions.q: The specific part of an antigen that binds to an antibody is called the
questions.x: An epitope is the small region of an antigen recognised by the antibody; the paratope is the matching site on the antibody.
questions.trap: Paratope is on the antibody, not the antigen.

questions.q: Cell-mediated immunity is carried out mainly by
questions.x: T cells act directly: cytotoxic T cells kill infected and cancer cells. B cells and plasma cells give humoral (antibody) immunity.

questions.q: A benign tumour differs from a malignant tumour in that a benign tumour
o: Stays localised and does not spread to other parts
Spreads to distant organs by metastasis
questions.x: Benign tumours remain confined; malignant (cancerous) tumours invade nearby tissues and metastasise. Oncology studies tumours (neoplasms).

questions.s: Medical technology: tissue and organ transplantation
questions.q: Skin taken from a patient's own thigh to cover a burn on the arm is an
questions.x: Autograft: donor and recipient are the same person, so no rejection. Isograft: identical twin; allograft: another human; xenograft: another species.

questions.s: Medical technology: tissue and organ transplantation
questions.q: After an organ transplant, cyclosporin A is given to
o: Kill bacteria in the new organ
Increase blood supply to the organ
Suppress the immune response and prevent rejection
questions.x: Cyclosporin A, obtained from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum, inhibits T-cell activation and is used as an immunosuppressant.

questions.s: Medical technology: tissue and organ transplantation
questions.q: Before a kidney transplant, donor and recipient are tissue-matched mainly for
questions.x: Graft rejection is a T-cell response to foreign HLA (MHC) antigens; closer HLA and ABO matching means less rejection.

questions.q: In in-vitro fertilisation (IVF, 'test-tube baby'), fertilisation takes place
o: Outside the body in a laboratory dish
Inside the test tube for the whole pregnancy
In the fallopian tube of the mother
In the uterus after artificial insemination
questions.x: Eggs and sperms are joined in the laboratory; the early embryo is then transferred into the mother's uterus or fallopian tube to develop.
questions.trap: Only fertilisation and early cleavage occur outside; the pregnancy is in the uterus.

questions.q: In ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), a technique used with IVF,
o: Sperms are placed in the uterus
A single sperm is injected directly into the ovum
An embryo is placed in the fallopian tube
The ovum is injected into the testis
questions.x: ICSI helps when sperm count or motility is very low: one selected sperm is injected straight into the egg cytoplasm.

questions.q: Amniocentesis is the
o: Removal of the placenta after birth
Injection of hormones to induce labour
Withdrawal of a small sample of amniotic fluid to study foetal cells
Transfer of an embryo into the uterus
questions.x: A needle draws amniotic fluid (usually at 15–20 weeks); foetal cells in it are cultured and their chromosomes and chemistry studied.

questions.q: Amniocentesis is used mainly to detect
o: High blood pressure in the mother
Chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome in the foetus
questions.x: Karyotyping foetal cells reveals aneuploidies like trisomy 21. Its misuse for sex determination is banned.

questions.q: An animal whose genome carries a deliberately introduced foreign gene is called a
questions.x: Transgenic animals (e.g. transgenic cows, mice) express foreign genes; a clone such as Dolly is a genetic copy, not necessarily transgenic.
questions.trap: Dolly was a clone, not transgenic.

questions.q: Rosie, the first transgenic cow (1997), produced milk enriched with
questions.x: Rosie's milk contained human α-lactalbumin (about 2.4 g/L), making it nutritionally closer to human milk for babies.

questions.q: Transgenic animals are useful in medicine mainly because they can
o: Produce human proteins and serve as models for human diseases
questions.x: Transgenic animals make useful proteins (e.g. α-1-antitrypsin) in milk, act as disease models and test vaccine safety.

questions.q: Milk is converted into curd by
questions.x: Lactic acid bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid, which coagulates milk proteins; they also raise vitamin B₁₂ content.

questions.q: Beer and wine are produced by fermentation of sugars using
questions.x: Brewer's yeast ferments sugars anaerobically into ethanol and CO₂.

questions.q: The large holes in Swiss cheese are made by CO₂ released by
questions.x: Propionibacterium shermanii ferments lactate, releasing CO₂ bubbles that form the characteristic holes ('eyes').

questions.s: Applied microbiology: sewage and drinking water treatment
questions.q: In secondary (biological) sewage treatment, organic matter is broken down mainly by
o: Aerobic microbes growing as flocs in aeration tanks
questions.x: Air is pumped in; aerobic bacteria and fungi form flocs that digest organic matter and lower BOD. Settled sludge goes to anaerobic digesters.

questions.s: Applied microbiology: sewage and drinking water treatment
questions.q: In anaerobic sludge digesters of a sewage plant, bacteria produce
questions.x: Anaerobic bacteria digest the activated sludge and release a gas mixture of methane, H₂S and CO₂ (biogas), usable as fuel.

questions.s: Applied microbiology: sewage and drinking water treatment
questions.q: A high BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) of a water sample indicates
o: High organic pollution of the water
questions.x: BOD measures oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter; more organic waste gives a higher BOD.
questions.trap: High BOD means oxygen is being used up, not that it is plentiful.

questions.s: Applied microbiology: sewage and drinking water treatment
questions.q: Chlorination of drinking water is done to
questions.x: Chlorine is a cheap disinfectant that kills bacteria in water; sedimentation and filtration remove mud.

questions.q: The fish Gambusia is used as a biological control agent against
questions.x: Gambusia (mosquito fish) eats mosquito larvae, reducing malaria and dengue vectors without chemicals.

questions.q: Bacillus thuringiensis is used as a bio-pesticide because it produces
o: Hormones that make plants grow faster
Cry proteins that are toxic to insect larvae
questions.x: Bt makes a crystal (Cry) protoxin that becomes active in the alkaline gut of insect larvae and kills them; it is harmless to humans.

questions.q: Trichoderma is used as a bio-control agent against
questions.x: Trichoderma, a free-living soil fungus, attacks and suppresses many plant-pathogenic fungi in the root zone.

questions.q: Mucin, the main substance of mucus secreted by salivary glands and goblet cells, is chemically a
questions.x: Mucins are heavily glycosylated proteins; the slimy mucus they form lubricates food and protects the gut lining from acid and enzymes.

questions.q: Humans can pass urine that is hypertonic (more concentrated) than blood mainly because of
o: Cortical nephrons with short loops of Henle
Juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops of Henle dipping deep into the medulla
questions.x: Long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons with the vasa recta build a high osmotic gradient in the medulla (counter-current); ADH then lets water leave the collecting duct.
questions.trap: Less ADH makes urine dilute, not concentrated.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: A person cannot move the jaw muscles used for chewing. The cranial nerve most likely damaged is the
questions.x: The mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (a mixed nerve) supplies the muscles of mastication. IV and VI move the eyeball; VIII carries hearing and balance.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Which group contains only purely sensory cranial nerves?
questions.x: I, II and VIII carry impulses only towards the brain (smell, sight, hearing and balance); damage to the olfactory nerve or bulb causes loss of smell. III, IV, VI, XI, XII are motor; V, VII, IX, X are mixed.

questions.q: Which gland is often nicknamed the '4S gland' because its hormones regulate salt, sugar, sex and stress?
questions.x: Adrenal cortex: aldosterone (salt), cortisol (sugar), sex corticoids (sex); adrenal medulla: adrenaline (stress). The pituitary is the 'master gland'.

questions.q: Which part of the adrenal gland is essential for life, so that its complete removal is fatal?
questions.x: Without corticoids (aldosterone, cortisol) the body loses Na⁺ and water and cannot hold blood pressure and sugar, so they are called life-saving hormones. Medullary adrenaline is the 'emergency' hormone.
questions.trap: Adrenaline is the emergency (fight-or-flight) hormone, but life goes on without the medulla.

questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure
questions.q: A substance that, if introduced into the bloodstream, would start coagulation of blood at that site is
questions.x: Thromboplastin (tissue factor) starts the clotting cascade: with Ca²⁺ it turns prothrombin into thrombin, which converts fibrinogen into fibrin. Heparin and citrate prevent clotting; plasmin dissolves clots.

questions.q: The testes of man lie in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity, because
o: Sperm formation needs a temperature about 2–3 °C lower than body temperature
Sperms mature faster at body temperature
Testosterone acts only outside the body cavity
There is no space for them in the abdomen
questions.x: The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than the body core; testes that fail to descend (cryptorchidism) cannot produce sperms, causing sterility.

questions.q: A breast-fed infant passes yellow stools. The colour comes mainly from
o: Bile pigments (bilirubin) poured into the gut with bile
questions.x: Bile pigments from haemoglobin breakdown colour the faeces. In infants, with few gut bacteria, bilirubin stays yellow; later bacteria change it to brown stercobilin.

questions.q: When blood glucose is so high that filtered glucose exceeds the tubular transport maximum (Tm),
o: The tubules reabsorb all the extra glucose
Filtration of glucose stops at the glomerulus
Reabsorption cannot rise any further and the excess glucose appears in urine
The loop of Henle secretes the extra glucose back into blood
questions.x: Glucose carriers of the PCT become saturated at Tm, so reabsorption stays at its maximum; above the renal threshold (about 180 mg/100 mL blood) glucose spills into urine (glycosuria).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of sodium ions in the human body?
o: Producing the action potential of nerve fibres
Maintaining osmotic pressure of extracellular fluid
Helping absorption of glucose in the intestine
Forming the oxygen-binding part of haemoglobin
questions.x: Na⁺ is the main ECF cation: it controls osmotic balance, its influx depolarises neurons, and Na⁺–glucose co-transport absorbs glucose. Iron, not sodium, binds O₂ in haem.

questions.q: Intraocular pressure, which is raised in glaucoma, is measured with a
questions.x: A tonometer measures pressure inside the eyeball. Sphygmomanometer: blood pressure; spirometer: lung volumes; audiometer: hearing.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes malaria from dengue?
o: Both are caused by viruses spread by Culex
Malaria is caused by a protozoan spread by Anopheles; dengue by a virus spread by Aedes
Malaria is caused by a virus; dengue by a protozoan
Dengue is spread by Anopheles; malaria by Aedes
questions.x: Malaria: Plasmodium (protozoan), female Anopheles, treated with antimalarial drugs. Dengue: dengue virus, Aedes aegypti, no specific antiviral drug.

questions.q: Which pair consists only of viral diseases?
questions.x: Common cold (rhinovirus) and herpes (herpes simplex virus) are viral. Malaria is protozoan; typhoid and tuberculosis are bacterial.

questions.q: Active pulmonary tuberculosis is confirmed by
o: Microscopic examination of sputum for acid-fast bacilli
questions.x: Ziehl–Neelsen stained sputum shows Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast bacilli). The Mantoux test only shows infection or exposure, not active disease.

questions.q: Identical antibodies produced by a hybridoma (a myeloma cell fused with a B-lymphocyte) are called
questions.x: One B-cell clone, made immortal by fusion with a myeloma cell, secretes one kind of antibody against one epitope; used in diagnosis (e.g. pregnancy kits) and therapy.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: The opening of the stomach into the duodenum is guarded by the
questions.x: The pyloric sphincter controls the passage of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum. The cardiac sphincter guards the oesophagus–stomach junction.
questions.trap: Cardiac sphincter is at the upper (oesophageal) end of the stomach.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: The vermiform appendix arises from the
questions.x: The appendix is a narrow blind tube attached to the caecum, the first part of the large intestine; it is vestigial in humans.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: The longest part of the human small intestine is the
questions.x: Duodenum about 25 cm, jejunum about 2.5 m, ileum about 3.5 m. The caecum belongs to the large intestine.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Human teeth set in sockets of the jaw bones are described as
questions.x: Thecodont: each tooth sits in a bony socket. Human teeth are also heterodont (different types) and diphyodont (two sets: milk and permanent).
questions.trap: Monophyodont is wrong; humans have two sets of teeth.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: The largest salivary gland of man, which swells in mumps, is the
questions.x: The parotid lies below and in front of the ear and opens by Stensen's duct; the mumps virus inflames it.

questions.s: Digestive system: alimentary canal and digestive glands
questions.q: Meissner's (submucosal) nerve plexus of the gut wall lies in the
questions.x: Meissner's plexus in the submucosa controls glands and local blood flow; Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus lies between the muscle layers of the muscularis.
questions.trap: Auerbach's plexus, not Meissner's, lies in the muscularis.

questions.q: Which enzyme is NOT present in pancreatic juice?
questions.x: Pepsin comes from the stomach (as pepsinogen from chief cells). Pancreatic juice has trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, lipase and nucleases.

questions.q: The hormone secretin mainly stimulates the pancreas to release
o: A watery juice rich in bicarbonate
questions.x: Acid chyme in the duodenum releases secretin; the bicarbonate it calls for neutralises the acid. Cholecystokinin (CCK) calls for enzyme-rich juice and gall bladder contraction.
questions.trap: Enzyme-rich pancreatic juice is the action of CCK.

questions.q: Gastrin, secreted by G-cells of the stomach, mainly
o: Stimulates secretion of gastric juice (HCl and pepsinogen)
questions.x: Food in the stomach releases gastrin into blood; it stimulates parietal cells (HCl) and chief cells (pepsinogen) and stomach movements.

questions.q: A person whose gall bladder has been removed is advised to eat less fatty food at a time, mainly because
o: Pancreatic lipase is no longer secreted
Bile can no longer be stored and released in large amounts when fatty food arrives
Fat can no longer be absorbed into lacteals
questions.x: The liver still makes bile, but it now trickles continuously into the duodenum; without the stored reserve a heavy fatty meal is poorly emulsified.
questions.trap: The liver, not the gall bladder, makes bile.

questions.q: During swallowing, food is kept out of the larynx by the
questions.x: The leaf-like elastic epiglottis folds over the glottis while swallowing. The soft palate and uvula close the nasopharynx.

questions.q: Each lung is enclosed in a double membrane with fluid between its layers, called the
questions.x: Pleural fluid reduces friction during breathing. The pericardium covers the heart, the peritoneum lines the abdomen and the meninges cover the brain.

questions.q: Which of the following belongs to the respiratory (gas-exchange) zone rather than the conducting zone?
questions.x: The conducting zone (nose to terminal bronchioles) only carries, warms and cleans air. Gas exchange happens in respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli.

questions.q: A person has expiratory reserve volume 1000 mL and residual volume 1200 mL. The functional residual capacity is
questions.x: Functional residual capacity = air left after a normal expiration = ERV + RV = 1000 + 1200 = 2200 mL.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: Although its partial pressure gradient is small, CO₂ diffuses across the alveolar membrane easily because
o: CO₂ is a smaller molecule than O₂
The alveolar wall is impermeable to O₂
CO₂ is about 20–25 times more soluble than O₂
questions.x: Diffusion depends on solubility as well as the pressure gradient. CO₂ is far more soluble, so a gradient of only about 5 mm Hg is enough.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: One molecule of haemoglobin can carry at most
questions.x: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains, each with one haem group whose Fe²⁺ binds one O₂ molecule.

questions.s: Respiratory system: gas exchange and transport
questions.q: Each gram of haemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of O₂. Blood with 15 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL, fully saturated, carries about
questions.x: 15 × 1.34 = 20.1 ≈ 20 mL O₂ per 100 mL of blood (about 20 volumes per cent).

questions.q: The pneumotaxic centre, which limits inspiration and helps set the breathing rate, is located in the
questions.x: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons switches off inspiration; the basic rhythm comes from the medullary respiratory centre.
questions.trap: Medulla holds the rhythm centre, not the pneumotaxic centre.

questions.q: Peripheral chemoreceptors that respond mainly to a fall in blood O₂ are located in the
questions.x: Carotid bodies (at the carotid fork) and aortic bodies (on the aortic arch) sense low O₂ and send impulses to the respiratory centre. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla sense CO₂/H⁺.

questions.s: Respiratory system: concept of respiratory disorders
questions.q: Silicosis and asbestosis are
o: Occupational lung diseases caused by inhaling mineral dust
questions.x: Long exposure to silica or asbestos dust in mines and factories causes fibrosis of lung tissue, reducing gas exchange.

questions.s: Respiratory system: concept of respiratory disorders
questions.q: Bacterial pneumonia, in which alveoli fill with fluid and mucus, is commonly caused by
questions.x: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) inflames the alveoli; the fluid-filled alveoli reduce gas exchange. It spreads by droplets.

questions.q: The tricuspid valve lies between the
questions.x: Tricuspid (three cusps) guards the right atrioventricular opening; the bicuspid (mitral) guards the left. Semilunar valves guard the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

questions.q: The chordae tendineae of the heart
o: Conduct the cardiac impulse to the ventricles
Carry blood to the heart muscle
Prevent the atrioventricular valve cusps from turning into the atria during ventricular contraction
questions.x: Papillary muscles pull on these tendinous cords so the tricuspid and bicuspid cusps do not evert when ventricular pressure rises.

questions.q: During the cardiac cycle, the semilunar valves open when
o: Ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary trunk
questions.x: In ventricular systole the AV valves close first; when ventricular pressure rises above arterial pressure the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected.

questions.q: In a cardiac cycle of 0.8 s, ventricular systole lasts about
questions.x: Typical values: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, joint diastole 0.4 s; total 0.8 s at 75 beats/min.
questions.trap: 0.4 s is the joint (complete) diastole.

questions.q: A heart has end-diastolic volume 120 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL, and beats 70 times a minute. Its cardiac output is
questions.x: Stroke volume = 120 − 50 = 70 mL. Cardiac output = 70 mL × 70/min = 4900 mL/min = 4.9 L/min.
questions.trap: 8.4 L/min uses 120 mL instead of the stroke volume.

questions.q: An artificial pacemaker is implanted mainly when
o: The blood group of the patient is rare
The SA node or conducting system fails to start or conduct impulses properly
questions.x: A pacemaker gives regular electrical impulses to the heart muscle, replacing a failing SA node or a heart block in the conducting pathway.

questions.q: In a normal ECG, the P wave represents
questions.x: P wave: atrial depolarisation (leads to atrial contraction); QRS: ventricular depolarisation; T wave: ventricular repolarisation.
questions.trap: QRS, not P, is ventricular depolarisation.

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: The only artery that carries deoxygenated blood in an adult is the
questions.x: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: The coronary sinus, which collects blood from the heart wall, opens into the
questions.x: Coronary veins drain into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium; its opening is guarded by the Thebesian (coronary) valve.

questions.s: Circulatory system: arterial and venous system
questions.q: In a healthy person, the blood with the lowest concentration of urea is found in the
questions.x: Urea made in the liver enters blood through the hepatic vein (highest urea); the kidneys remove it, so blood leaving them in the renal vein has the least.
questions.trap: Hepatic vein has the most urea, because the liver makes it.

questions.s: Circulatory system: blood group and pressure
questions.q: A person of blood group A can safely receive blood of group
questions.x: Group A plasma has anti-B antibodies, so donated red cells must lack the B antigen: groups A and O.

questions.q: Blood pressure is routinely measured with a sphygmomanometer on the
o: Brachial artery of the upper arm
questions.x: The cuff is wrapped round the upper arm and sounds are heard over the brachial artery at heart level.
questions.trap: The radial artery is used for counting the pulse, not for BP.

questions.q: Chest pain that comes on during exertion because heart muscle gets too little oxygen is called
questions.x: Narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough O₂ when the heart works harder; the pain eases with rest. Complete blockage causes a heart attack.

questions.q: The columns of Bertini of the kidney are
o: Collecting ducts that open into the pelvis
Parts of the loop of Henle
Extensions of cortex between the medullary pyramids
questions.x: Renal cortex dips between the pyramids of the medulla as columns of Bertini; the pyramids open by papillae into calyces.

questions.q: ADH (vasopressin) increases water reabsorption by
o: Making the distal tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water
Increasing active transport of glucose in the PCT
Making the ascending limb permeable to water
questions.x: ADH inserts water channels (aquaporins) into DCT and collecting duct cells, so water leaves into the hypertonic medulla and urine becomes concentrated.

questions.q: In tubular secretion, the tubule cells add to the filtrate substances such as
questions.x: Secretion removes extra H⁺ and K⁺ (helping pH and ion balance) and some wastes and drugs. Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, not secreted.

questions.q: Normal glomerular filtrate differs from blood plasma mainly in lacking
questions.x: The filtration membrane holds back blood cells and large proteins; small solutes such as glucose, urea and ions pass freely.

questions.q: If the glomerular filtration rate is 120 mL per minute, the volume of filtrate formed in one day is about
questions.x: 120 mL/min × 60 × 24 = 172 800 mL ≈ 173 L per day; about 99% of it is reabsorbed.

questions.q: When blood volume and pressure rise, the atria release atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which
o: Increases Na⁺ and water excretion and lowers blood pressure
questions.x: ANF opposes the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system: it dilates vessels and promotes loss of Na⁺ and water in urine.

questions.s: Excretory system: concept of renal disorders
questions.q: Large amounts of albumin in the urine (proteinuria) most likely indicate damage to the
questions.x: Plasma proteins are normally too large to pass the glomerular membrane; damage to it lets albumin into the filtrate.

questions.s: Excretory system: concept of renal disorders
questions.q: Ketone bodies appear in the urine (ketonuria) in
o: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus or prolonged starvation
questions.x: When cells cannot use glucose, fat is broken down rapidly and ketone bodies accumulate in blood and spill into urine.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted mainly by the
o: Choroid plexuses in the ventricles of the brain
questions.x: Choroid plexuses (vascular folds of pia mater) form CSF; arachnoid villi return it to venous blood. CSF cushions and nourishes the brain.
questions.trap: Arachnoid villi absorb CSF; they do not secrete it.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Which effect is produced by stimulation of the parasympathetic nervous system?
o: Increased secretion of saliva and digestive juices
questions.x: Parasympathetic ('rest and digest'): slows the heart, constricts pupils and stimulates gut secretions and movements. The other three are sympathetic effects.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The correct path of impulses in a spinal reflex arc is
o: Receptor → motor neuron → spinal cord → sensory neuron → effector
Receptor → sensory neuron → interneuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector
Effector → sensory neuron → brain → motor neuron → receptor
questions.x: A reflex arc passes through the spinal cord without needing the brain, so the response (e.g. knee jerk, withdrawal) is quick and involuntary.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: In the spinal cord,
o: Grey matter is outside and white matter inside
Grey matter is inside (butterfly-shaped) and white matter is outside
Grey and white matter are evenly mixed
questions.x: The spinal cord has an inner H-shaped grey matter of cell bodies surrounded by white matter of myelinated tracts, the reverse of the cerebral cortex.
questions.trap: Grey outside, white inside is the arrangement in the cerebrum.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: Broca's area, damage to which affects the production of speech, lies in the
questions.x: Broca's motor speech area is in the frontal lobe (usually left). Occipital lobe: vision; temporal lobe: hearing.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The tree-like branching of white matter called 'arbor vitae' is seen in the
questions.x: In a section of the cerebellum, white matter branches inside the grey cortex like a tree, hence 'tree of life'.

questions.s: Nervous system: CNS, PNS and autonomic
questions.q: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve is cut. The most likely result in the area it supplies is
o: Loss of movement, with sensation intact
Loss of sensation, with movement still possible
Loss of both sensation and movement
No change, since the ventral root takes over
questions.x: Dorsal roots carry sensory (afferent) fibres into the cord; ventral roots carry motor fibres out. Cutting only the dorsal root removes sensation.
questions.trap: Loss of movement follows damage to the ventral root.

questions.q: Repolarisation of a neuron after an action potential is mainly due to
