questions.x: After Na⁺ channels close, voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves, bringing the inside back to negative.
questions.trap: Na⁺ inflow causes depolarisation, not repolarisation.

questions.q: According to the all-or-none law, a stimulus much stronger than threshold produces in a single nerve fibre
o: An action potential that travels backwards
An action potential of the same size as a threshold stimulus
questions.x: Once threshold is reached the fibre fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not increase the size of the action potential, only the frequency of impulses.

questions.q: Acetylcholine released at a synapse is broken down by the enzyme
questions.x: Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending the signal so the next impulse can pass.

questions.q: Release of neurotransmitter from the axon terminal is triggered by entry of
questions.x: The arriving impulse opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ entry makes synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane and release their contents.

questions.q: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is corrected by using a
questions.x: In hypermetropia the eyeball is short, so near images form behind the retina; a converging (convex) lens brings them forward.
questions.trap: Concave lens corrects myopia.

questions.q: The fovea centralis (yellow spot) gives the sharpest vision because it has
o: Equal numbers of rods and cones
questions.x: The fovea contains closely packed cones each with its own nerve fibre, giving fine detail and colour in bright light. The blind spot has no receptors.

questions.q: The correct path of light through the eye to the retina is
o: Cornea → aqueous humour → lens → vitreous humour
Lens → cornea → vitreous humour → aqueous humour
Cornea → vitreous humour → lens → aqueous humour
Aqueous humour → cornea → lens → vitreous humour
questions.x: Aqueous humour fills the space between cornea and lens; jelly-like vitreous humour fills the space between lens and retina.

questions.q: Presbyopia, common after about 40 years of age, is due to
o: Loss of elasticity of the lens, so near objects are not focused
Lack of cones in the retina
questions.x: With age the lens hardens and cannot become rounder for near vision; reading glasses with convex lenses help.

questions.q: The footplate of the stapes fits into the
questions.x: Stapes vibrations at the oval window set the perilymph of the cochlea in motion; the round window bulges out to release the pressure.

questions.q: The fluid that fills the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear is
questions.x: Endolymph is inside the membranous labyrinth; perilymph lies between the membranous and bony labyrinths.
questions.trap: Perilymph surrounds, rather than fills, the membranous labyrinth.

questions.q: The maculae of the utriculus and sacculus detect
o: Position of the head with respect to gravity (static balance)
questions.x: Hair cells of the macula carry otoliths (CaCO₃ crystals) that shift with gravity and linear movement. Rotation is detected by cristae; sound by the organ of Corti.

questions.q: The sensory hair cells of the organ of Corti rest on the
questions.x: Hair cells sit on the basilar membrane; their hairs touch the overhanging tectorial membrane. Vibration bends the hairs and starts nerve impulses.
questions.trap: The tectorial membrane lies over, not under, the hair cells.

questions.q: A person's cochlea is damaged but the semicircular canals and vestibule are normal. The person will have
o: Loss of balance with normal hearing
Loss of both hearing and balance
Loss of hearing with normal balance
questions.x: The cochlea (organ of Corti) serves hearing; the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, utriculus, sacculus) serves balance.

questions.q: Besides connecting the middle ear with the pharynx, the Eustachian tube
o: Carries sound waves to the cochlea
Drains endolymph from the inner ear
Holds the ear ossicles in place
Equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum
questions.x: Swallowing or yawning opens the tube so middle-ear pressure matches outside air; this is why ears 'pop' in aircraft or on mountain roads.

questions.q: Glucagon, which raises blood glucose, is secreted by the
o: α-cells of the islets of Langerhans
β-cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.x: α-cells make glucagon (stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver); β-cells make insulin; δ-cells make somatostatin. Acinar cells make digestive enzymes.
questions.trap: β-cells secrete insulin, the glucose-lowering hormone.

questions.q: Calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium, is secreted by the
questions.x: Calcitonin from thyroid C-cells moves Ca²⁺ into bone; parathormone does the opposite. Follicular cells make thyroxine (T₄) and T₃.
questions.trap: Parathyroid hormone raises, not lowers, blood calcium.

questions.q: Simple (endemic) goitre, common in hilly areas, is caused mainly by
o: Deficiency of iodine in the diet
questions.x: Without iodine little thyroxine is made; high TSH then enlarges the thyroid. Iodised salt prevents it.

questions.q: Hyposecretion of thyroxine in adults causes
questions.x: Adult hypothyroidism: low metabolic rate, puffy skin, weight gain, sluggishness. Cretinism is the childhood form; exophthalmic goitre is hyperthyroidism.
questions.trap: Cretinism is thyroxine deficiency in children, not adults.

questions.q: Tetany, with painful muscle spasms due to low blood calcium, results from
questions.x: Parathormone raises blood Ca²⁺; when it is deficient Ca²⁺ falls and nerves and muscles become over-excitable.

questions.q: A child is very short but has normal intelligence and normal body proportions. The most likely cause is
o: Deficiency of growth hormone in childhood
questions.x: Pituitary dwarfism: proportionate short stature with normal mind. Childhood thyroxine deficiency (cretinism) also stunts growth but with mental retardation.
questions.trap: Cretinism also causes short stature, but intelligence is impaired.

questions.q: Which of the following hormones is a steroid?
questions.x: Cortisol (adrenal cortex) and sex hormones are steroids made from cholesterol. Insulin and oxytocin are peptides; adrenaline is an amine.

questions.q: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which controls FSH and LH release, is secreted by the
questions.x: Hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal system and control its secretion of tropic hormones.

questions.q: After childbirth, milk production (synthesis) by the mammary glands is stimulated by
questions.x: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary makes the glands produce milk; oxytocin from the posterior pituitary ejects (lets down) the milk.
questions.trap: Oxytocin causes milk ejection, not milk production.

questions.q: A patient passes very large volumes of dilute urine that contains no glucose. The most likely cause is
questions.x: Without ADH the collecting ducts stay impermeable to water, so much dilute urine is lost (diabetes insipidus). Insulin deficiency also causes polyuria but with glucose in urine.
questions.trap: Insulin deficiency causes polyuria with glycosuria.

questions.q: Sperms are stored and become motile (mature) in the
questions.x: From the seminiferous tubules sperms pass via vasa efferentia to the coiled epididymis, where they are stored and gain motility.

questions.q: The fluid of the seminal vesicles is rich in fructose, which
o: Forms the outer coat of the sperm
Provides energy for the swimming sperms
questions.x: Fructose in seminal fluid is the main energy source for sperm motility. The prostate adds a milky fluid; Cowper's glands secrete lubricating mucus.

questions.q: Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands of the male secrete
questions.x: These paired glands release a clear alkaline mucus into the urethra before ejaculation for lubrication and neutralising traces of urine.

questions.q: Unlike spermatogenesis, which begins at puberty, oogenesis
o: Begins before birth, with primary oocytes arrested in prophase I
Begins at puberty and continues throughout life
questions.x: Oogonia multiply in the foetal ovary and enter meiosis; primary oocytes stay in prophase I until puberty, when one completes meiosis I each cycle.

questions.q: In human oogenesis, meiosis II of the secondary oocyte is completed only
questions.x: The secondary oocyte is ovulated arrested at metaphase II; sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II, forming the ovum and the second polar body.

questions.q: The first polar body is formed when
o: The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II
The primary oocyte completes meiosis I
questions.x: Meiosis I divides the primary oocyte unequally into a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body.

questions.q: The chromosome numbers in a human primary spermatocyte and a spermatid are respectively
questions.x: Primary spermatocytes are diploid (2n = 46); meiosis I makes haploid secondary spermatocytes (23), and meiosis II gives spermatids (23).

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: The phase of the menstrual cycle in which the endometrium regenerates and thickens under oestrogen is the
questions.x: After menstruation, oestrogen from growing follicles rebuilds the endometrium; after ovulation, progesterone makes it secretory.
questions.trap: Secretory phase follows ovulation and depends on progesterone.

questions.s: Reproductive system: ovarian and menstrual cycle
questions.q: If fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum keeps secreting progesterone because it is maintained by
questions.x: hCG acts like LH, preventing the corpus luteum from degenerating, so progesterone keeps the endometrium and menstruation stops.

questions.q: The Salk polio vaccine (IPV), given by injection, contains
questions.x: Salk's IPV uses formalin-killed virus; Sabin's oral polio vaccine (OPV) uses live attenuated virus.
questions.trap: Live attenuated virus is in Sabin's oral vaccine.

questions.q: A toxoid used as a vaccine is
o: A bacterial toxin made harmless but still able to induce antibodies
A live bacterium with reduced virulence
questions.x: Toxins of tetanus and diphtheria bacteria are treated (e.g. with formalin) to lose toxicity while keeping antigenicity; the body then makes antitoxin antibodies.
questions.trap: Ready-made antibodies give passive immunity; that is antitoxin, not toxoid.

questions.q: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided in people with severely weakened immunity because
o: The weakened microbes may still multiply and cause disease in them
They act only by passive immunity
questions.x: Attenuated microbes multiply a little in the body; a normal immune system controls them, but in severe immunodeficiency they can cause the disease. Inactivated and toxoid vaccines are safer there.

questions.q: A condition that favours candidiasis is
o: A diet rich in vitamin C
questions.x: High sugar in body fluids, antibiotics, pregnancy and weak immunity (e.g. HIV) allow Candida albicans to overgrow; normal flora keeps it in check.

questions.q: Oral or vaginal candidiasis is treated with
o: Antifungal drugs such as nystatin or fluconazole
questions.x: Candida is a yeast-like fungus, so antibacterial antibiotics do not kill it; they may even make it worse by killing competing bacteria.
questions.trap: Penicillin is antibacterial and does not act on fungi.

questions.q: Vibrio cholerae, the cause of cholera, is a
questions.x: Vibrio is curved like a comma and motile by a single flagellum; it spreads through faecally contaminated water and food.

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes severe watery diarrhoea mainly by
o: Destroying the villi of the small intestine
Making intestinal cells secrete Cl⁻ and water into the gut lumen
Making the colon absorb more water
questions.x: The toxin raises cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells, which pump out Cl⁻; Na⁺ and water follow, causing rice-water stools. The gut lining stays intact, so ORS works.

questions.q: The surface spikes of the influenza virus, whose changes produce new strains, are
questions.x: Strain names such as H1N1 refer to these two envelope glycoproteins; antigenic drift and shift change them.

questions.q: Antibiotics such as penicillin do not cure influenza because
o: Influenza is caused by a fungus
The influenza bacterium has a thick capsule
Influenza is caused by a virus
questions.x: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures like cell walls and 70S ribosomes, which viruses lack. They may be given only for secondary bacterial infection.

questions.q: Hepatitis D virus can cause infection only in a person who is also infected with
questions.x: HDV is a defective RNA virus that needs the surface antigen (HBsAg) of HBV for its coat; the hepatitis B vaccine therefore also protects against hepatitis D.

questions.q: Among the hepatitis viruses A to E, the one with a DNA genome is
questions.x: HBV is a partly double-stranded DNA virus; hepatitis A, C, D and E viruses all have RNA genomes.

questions.q: In typhoid, ulceration and sometimes perforation of the intestine occur mainly at the
questions.x: Salmonella typhi invades the lymphoid Peyer's patches of the ileum; their ulceration can bleed or perforate in the third week of illness.

questions.q: A typhoid 'carrier' is a person who
o: Has typhoid fever with high fever
Harbours Salmonella typhi, often in the gall bladder, and sheds it without being ill
questions.x: Carriers pass bacteria in faeces for months or years, so they can infect others through food they handle. 'Typhoid Mary' was a famous example.

questions.q: Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads from person to person mainly through
o: Droplets coughed or sneezed into the air
questions.x: Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum droplets is inhaled by others; crowded, poorly ventilated places favour its spread.

questions.q: The 'window period' in HIV infection is the time when
o: The virus is present but antibody tests are still negative
questions.x: Antibodies take some weeks to appear after infection; in this period an ELISA can be negative though the person is infectious.
questions.trap: The person is infectious during the window period.

questions.q: Interferons, released by virus-infected cells,
o: Are antibodies made by plasma cells
Kill bacteria by breaking their cell walls
Make neighbouring cells resistant to viral multiplication
questions.x: Interferons are proteins of innate immunity; they are not virus-specific and act by inducing antiviral proteins in nearby cells.
